# Pre-Trained Language Models for Interactive Decision-Making

## Abstract



Pre-Trained Language Models for Interactive Decision-Making

 Anonymous Author(s) AffiliationAddress email

Abstract Language model (LM) pre-training is useful in many language processing tasks. 1 But can pre-trained LMs be further leveraged for more general machine learn- 2 ing problems? We propose an approach for using LMs to scaffold learning and 3 generalization in general sequential decision-making problems. In this approach, 4 goals and observations are represented as a sequence of embeddings, and a policy 5 network initialized with a pre-trained LM predicts the next action. We demonstrate 6 that this framework enables effective combinatorial generalization across differ- 7 ent environments and supervisory modalities. We begin by assuming access to 8 a set of expert demonstrations, and show that initializing policies with LMs and 9 fine-tuning them via behavior cloning improves task completion rates by 43.6% 10 in the VirtualHome environment. We then examine how our framework may be 11 used in environments without pre-collected expert data. To do this, we integrate 12 an active data gathering procedure into pre-trained LMs. The agent iteratively 13 learns by interacting with the environment, relabeling the language goal of past 14 “failed” experiences, and updating the policy in a self-supervised loop. The ac- 15 tive data gathering procedure also enables effective combinatorial generalization, 16 outperforming the best baseline by 25.1%. Finally, we explain these results by 17 investigating three possible factors underlying the effectiveness of the LM-based 18 policy. We find that sequential input representations (vs. fixed-dimensional feature 19 vectors) and favorable weight initialization are both important for generalization. 20 Surprisingly, however, the format of the policy inputs encoding (e.g. as a natural 21 language string vs. an arbitrary sequential encoding) has little influence. Together, 22 these results suggest that language modeling induces representations that are useful 23 for modeling not just language, but also goals and plans; these representations can 24 aid learning and generalization even outside of language processing. 25



1 Introduction 26

 Language models (LMs) play a key role in machine learning approaches to natural language 27 processing tasks [8]. This includes tasks that are not purely linguistic, and require nontrivial planning 28 and reasoning capabilities [24, 12]: for example, instruction following, vision-language navigation, 29 and visual question answering. Indeed, some of these tasks are so distant from language modeling 30 that one can ask whether pre-trained LMs can be used as a general framework even for tasks that 31 involve no language at all. If so, how might these capabilities be accessed in a model trained only to 32 process and generate natural language strings? 33 In this paper, we study these questions through the lens of embodied decision-making , investigating 34 the effectiveness of LM pre-training as a general framework for learning policies across a variety of 35 environments. As shown in Figure 1 (right), we encode the inputs to a policy—including 37 observations, goals, and history—as a sequence of embeddings. These embeddings are passed to a 38 policy network initialized with the parameters of a pre-trained LM, which is fine-tuned to predict 39 actions. This framework is generic, accommodating goals and environment states represented as 40 natural language strings, image patches, or scene graphs. 41 We find that imitation learning using pre-trained LMs as policy initializers improves in-domain 42 performance and enables strong generalization over novel tasks. For i.i.d. training and evaluation tasks, 43 this approach yields 20% more successful policies than other baseline methods in VirtualHome [29]. 44 For combinatorial generalization to out-of-distribution tasks, i.e . tasks involving new combinations 45 of goals, states or objects, LM pre-training confers even more benefits: it improves task completion 46 rates by 43.6% for tasks involving novel tasks (see Figure 3). These results hold for a variety of 47 environment representations: encoding states as natural language strings, when possible, improves 48 the data-efficiency of training, but even LMs fine-tuned on random environment encodings generalize 49 combinatorially to new goals and states when trained on large enough datasets. 50 We further examine how our method may be used in environments, where the expert data is not 51 available and an agent must actively gather data from the surrounding environment. To do this, we 52 integrate an A ctive D ata G athering ( ADG ) procedure into pretrained LMs as shown in Figure 2. The 53 proposed method with ADG consists of three parts. First, exploration collects trajectories using a 54 mix of random actions and actions generated by the current policy. Exploration is insufficient in 55 this high dimensional problem and most of the trajectories will likely fail to achieve the end goal. 56 A key insight is that even the failed trajectories contain useful sub-trajectories that solve certain 57 sub-goals, and we relabel their goal in the hindsight relabeling stage. The relabeled goal describes 58 what was achieved in the extracted sub-trajectory. Policy update samples relabeled trajectories to 59 update the policy. The active data gathering procedure allows us to train the LM-policy without 60 pre-collected expert data. It also outperforms the Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods on embodied 61 decision-making tasks and enables more effective generalization to novel tasks. 62 We hypothesize and investigate three possible factors underlying the effectiveness of pre-trained 63 LM for generalization in policy learning: 1) input encoding scheme; 2) sequential input represen- 64 tations; and 3) favorable weights initialization. We investigate 1) by encoding the policy inputs as 65 different types of sequences. Different input encoding schemes have only a negligible impact on the 66 performance: the effectiveness of language modeling is not limited to utilizing natural strings, but in 67 fact extends to arbitrary sequential encodings. We study 2) by encoding observations with a single 68 vector embedding, thereby removing its sequential structure. This operation significantly degrades 69 the model’s performance on novel tasks. Finally, we investigate 3) by learning the parameters of the 70 policy from scratch. The success rate after removing the pre-trained LM weights drops by 11 . 2% . 71 To summarize, our work has four main contributions. 72 • First, we propose to use pre-trained LMs as a general scaffold for interactive decision-making 73 across a variety of environments by converting all policy inputs into sequential data. 74 • Second, the proposed method demonstrates that language modeling improves combinatorial 75 generalization in policy learning : initializing a policy with a pre-trained LM substantially 76 improves out-of-distribution performance on novel tasks. 77 2 • Third, we integrate an active data gathering procedure into the proposed approach to further 78 enable policy learning on environments without using pre-collected expert data. 79 • Finally, we perform several analyses to explain the generalization capabilities of pre-trained LMs, 80 finding that natural strings are not needed to benefit from LM pre-training, but the sequential input 81 encoding and weight pre-training are important. 82 These results point to the effectiveness of the proposed framework with pre-trained LMs as a general- 83 purpose framework to promote structured generalization in interactive decision-making. 84

2 Related Work

 85 In recent years, word and sentence representations from pre-trained LMs [27, 8, 31] have become 86 ubiquitous in natural language processing [45, 28]. Some of the most successful applications of 87 pre-training lie at the boundary of natural language processing and other domains, as in instruction 88 following [12] and language-guided image retrieval [22]. 89 Learning representations of language. From nearly the earliest days of the field, natural language 90 processing researchers observed that representations of words derived from distributional statistics in 91 large text corpora serve as useful features for downstream tasks [7, 10]. The earliest versions of these 92 representation learning schemes focused on isolated word forms [25, 26]. However, recent years have 93 seen a number of techniques for training (masked or autoregressive) language models to produce 94 contextualized word representations (which incorporate information neighboring words in sentences 95 and paragraphs) via a variety of masked-word prediction objectives [8, 43]. 96 Applications of pre-trained LMs. LMs can be fine-tuned to perform language processing tasks 97 other than language modeling by casting those tasks as word-prediction problems. Successful uses 98 of representations from pre-trained models include syntactic parsing [19] and language-to-code 99 translation [41]; successful adaptations of LM prediction heads include machine translation [45], 100 sentiment classification [5] and style transfer [18]. A number of tasks integrate language and other 101 modalities, including visual question answering and image captioning [44]. Recent works find that 102 image representations can be injected directly into LMs’ embedding layers [39]. 103 LM pre-training beyond language The possibility that LMs might encode non-linguistic information 104 useful for other downstream tasks is suggested by a number of recent studies [34, 16, 21]. Several 105 recent papers [33, 17, 14] consider questions related to the ones investigated here. [5] show that the 106 GPT-3 model is capable of performing a limited set of arithmetic and string manipulation tasks; [23] 107 show that pre-trained LMs require very little fine-tuning to match the performance of task-specific 108 models on several image classification and numerical sequence processing tasks. [36] show that LMs 109 can serve as an effective backbone for hierarchical policies that express plans as natural language 110 strings [2, 4]. In this paper, we focus on building a general framework for decision-making tasks 111 using pre-trained LMs, even when language is not provided as an input or output. 112

3 Decision-Making and Language Modeling

 113

3.1 POMDPs and Policy Learning

 114 We explore the application of LMs to general sequential decision-making tasks in partially observed 115 environments. These tasks may be formalized as partially observable Markov decision processes 116 (POMDPs). A POMDP is defined by a set of states S , a set of observations O , a set of actions A , 117 and a transition model T ( s t +1 | s t , a t ) . Importantly, in a POMDP setting, the observation o t only 118 captures a portion of the underlying state s t , and an optimal decision-making strategy (a policy ) must 119 incorporate both the current observation and the previous history of observations and actions. In our 120 experiments, policies are parametric models π ϕ ( a t +1 | g, h t , o t ) that select actions given the goals g , 121 history information h t , and partial observations o t of the current state s t . 122 In Figure 1 (right), we show a high-level overview of the proposed method. We first convert all policy 123 inputs into a sequence and provide them as input to a transformer encoder. Representations from this 124 encoder model are then passed to a task-specific decoder that predicts actions. We collect a dataset of 125 N training trajectories D = { d 1 , · · · , d N } , where each individual trajectory consists of a goal and a 126 sequence of observations and actions: d i = { g i , o i 1 , a i 1 , · · · , o iT i , a iT i } , where T i is the length of the 127 trajectory. We then train the policy to maximize the probability p ( { a i } Ni =1 |D ) of actions we want to 128 achieve a i = { a i 1 , . . . , a iT i } across trajectories using the cross-entropy loss: 129 3 − ln p ( { a i } Ni =1 |D ) = − N (cid:88) i =1 T i (cid:88) t =1 ln p ( a it +1 | g i , h it , o it ) . (1) where h it represents the history information before time t . 130

3.2 Language models as policy initializers

 131 Our experiments focus on autoregressive , transformer-based LMs [40]. These models are trained 132 to fit a distribution p ( y ) over a text sequence y = { y 1 , y 2 , . . . , y n } via the chain rule p ( y ) = 133 p ( y 1 ) (cid:81) ni =2 p ( y i | y 1 , . . . , y i − 1 ) . Each term on the right hand side is parameterized by a transformer 134 network, which accepts the conditioned tokens as input. Each token passes through a learned 135 embedding layer F θ , then the full conditioned sequence is fed into the LM. In our work, we use a 136 standard LM, GPT-2, to process the input sequence rather than to predict future tokens. 137 Both POMDP decision-making and language modeling are naturally framed as sequence prediction 138 tasks, where successive words or actions/observations are predicted based on a sequence of previous 139 words or actions/observations. This suggests that pre-trained LMs can be used to initialize POMDP 140 policies by fine-tuning them to model high-reward or expert trajectories, as described below. 141

4 Approach

 142 We evaluate the effectiveness of pre-trained LMs in solving decision-making tasks across envi- 143 ronments. We use BabyAI [15] and VirtualHome [29] to evaluate the proposed method. While 144 both environments feature complex goals, the nature of these goals, as well as the state and action 145 sequences that accomplish them, differ substantially across environments (Figure 1 (left)). 146

4.1 Policy Network

 147 We first examine whether pre-trained LMs provide effective initializers when states and action 148 histories are represented as natural language strings. We encode the inputs to the policy—including 149 observations, goals, and action histories—as sequences of words. These word sequences are passed 150 to the LM (using its pre-trained word embedding layer F θ ) and used to obtain contextualized token 151 representations. These token representations are averaged and used to predict actions. We design a 152 policy network following the general policy framework proposed in Figure 1. 153 Environment encodings in VirtualHome. In VirtualHome, each goal consists of a sequence of pred- 154 icates and multiplicities, and is translated into a templated English sentence ( e.g . “ Inside(apple, 155 fridge):2 ” becomes “put two apples inside the fridge”). To encode the agent’s partial observation, 156 we extract a list of currently visible objects, their states ( e.g . “open, clean”), and 3D world coordinates. 157 We use a fully-connected layer to encode the 3D information and generate a feature representation of 158 each object in the observation. To encode history, we store information about all previous actions and 159 convert them into templated English sentences ( e.g . “I have put the plate on the kitchen table and the 160 apple inside the fridge”). 161 Environment encodings in BabyAI. The observation by default is a 7 × 7 grid. We convert the 162 observation into 7 × 7 text descriptions, e.g . “purple ball”, “grey wall”, “open door”, and combine 163 them into a long sentence. We then convert the history actions into text descriptions, e.g . “turn left” 164 and “go forward”. We combine the language instruction (without modification) with the observation 165 and history text descriptions, and feed them to the pre-trained LM. 166 We note that the policy network described above does not strictly require that these encodings take 167 the form of natural language strings—other encodings of the environment as a sequence also work 168 (see Section 7). This framework could be also generalized to support pixel-based observations using 169 discretization schemes like the one employed in the Vision Transformer [9]. 170 Action prediction. We pool the outputs of the pre-trained LM into a “context feature” that is used to 171 predict the next action. In training, we maximize the probabilities of actions we want to achieve. In 172 inference, we select the valid action with the highest probability. See Appendix D.1 for more details. 173 VirtualHome and BabyAI have quite different observation spaces , action spaces , and goal spaces; 174 however, we show that embedding policy inputs as sequences and utilizing the pre-trained LM as a 175 policy initializer, enables effective generalization to novel tasks on both environments. We note that 176 LID is not limited to VirtualHome and BabyAI, but is straightforwardly applicable to other embodied 177 environments, such as ALFRED [38] and iGibson [37]. 178 4

4.2 Data Gathering

 179 We first examine LID through imitation learning on data collected by experts in Section 4.2.1. We 180 then show that integrating an active data gathering procedure into LID enables policy learning without 181 using expert data in Section 4.2.2. We use VirtualHome as an example to explain the data gathering. 182

4.2.1 Policy Learning with Expert Data

 183 The policy model is first initialized from a pre-trained LM and then fine-tuned on data collected 184 by experts. We build on the VirtualHome environment to collect a set of expert trajectories using 185 regression planning [20] and create a VirtualHome-Imitation Learning dataset . Given a task 186 described by goal predicates, the planner generates an action sequence to accomplish this task (See 187 Appendix F.1 ). The planner has access to privileged information, such as information about the 188 pre-conditions and effects of each action, allowing an agent to robustly perform tasks in partially 189 observable environments and generate expert trajectories for training and evaluation. 190

4.2.2 Policy Learning with Active Data Gathering

 Collecting expert data is sometimes chal- 192 lenging. It may require privileged informa- 193 tion of the environment or human annota- 194 tions, which can be time-consuming and 195 difficult to scale. A promising way to scale 196 up supervision is Hindsight Experience Re- 197 play (HER) [3], which allows agents to 198 learn from orders of magnitude more data 199 without supervision . However, existing 200 HER methods [ 11] focus on simple tasks 201 with small state/action space and full ob- 202 servability. They cannot tackle more com- 203 plicated embodied decision-making tasks, 204 requiring nontrivial planning and reasoning 205 or natural language understanding. LID 206 with the active data gathering ( LID-ADG ) 207 can be used in solving tasks in such envi- 208 ronments. 209 As shown in Figure 2, LID-ADG consists of three components, i.e . exploration , hindsight relabeling , 210 and policy update . The key idea is to gradually improve the task success rate by asking the agent 211 to iteratively explore the environment, relabel failure samples, and update its policy using imitation 212 learning. In the exploration stage, we first randomly sample a goal g and an initial state s o . We 213 then use a mix of random actions and actions generated by the current policy π ϕ ( a t +1 | g, h t , o t ) to 214 obtain the next action a t +1 . We repeat this process until this episode ends. We collect M trajectories 215 and store them in the replay buffers. The generated actions in the early stages can barely finish the 216 given task. However, even the failed trajectories contain useful sub-trajectories that solve certain 217 sub-goals. In the hindsight relabeling stage, we extract useful sub-trajectories and relabel a goal g ′ 218 for each of them. We design a goal relabel function f l that generates a goal based on the sequence of 219 observations and actions using hand-designed templates. In practice, we implement the goal relabel 220 function as a program (see Appendix F.2 ). The hindsight relabeling stage allows sample-efficient 221 learning by reusing the failure cases. During policy update , the agent samples the data from the 222 replay buffers and updates its policy network π ϕ . 223 By interleaving the exploration, hindsight relabeling, and policy update, LID-ADG can gradually 224 improve the policy without requiring pre-collected expert data. In embodied environments with 225 large action spaces, sparse rewards, and long-horizon planning, RL methods often struggle to obtain 226 stable policy gradients during training. Our method enables sample-efficient learning from the sparse 227 rewards by relabeling new goals for the bad samples that the agent fails to achieve. In addition, 228 LID-ADG leverages the stability of supervised learning in the policy update stage, enabling it to 229 outperform RL approaches on a wide range of decision-making tasks. 230

5 Experiment Setup

 231 We evaluate the proposed method and baselines on VirtualHome and BabyAI. 232 5

5.1 VirtualHome 233

 VirtualHome is a 3D embodied environment featuring partial observability, large action spaces, and 234 long time horizons. We evaluate policies’ performance from three aspects: (1) performance on 235 in-distribution tasks; (2) generalization to novel scenes; and (3) generalization to novel tasks. 236 In-Distribution. The predicate types and their counts in the goal are randomly sampled from the 237 same distribution as the training data. The objects are initially placed in the environment according to 238 common-sense layouts; ( e.g . plates appear inside the kitchen cabinets rather than the bathtub). Novel 239 Scenes. The objects are placed in random positions in the initial environment without common-sense 240 constraints ( e.g . apples may appear inside the dishwasher). Novel Tasks. The components of all goal 241 predicates are never seen together during training ( e.g . both plates and fridge appear in training goals, 242 but Inside(plate, fridge) only appears in the test set. (See Appendix G for more details.) 243 We evaluate the success rates of different methods on each test set. A given episode is scored as 244 successful if the policy completes its entire goal within the maximum allowed steps of the environment. 245 On each of the 3 test subsets, we use 5 different random seeds and test 100 tasks under each seed. 246 Thus there are 1500 examples used to evaluate each model. 247

5.2 BabyAI

 248 BabyAI is a 2D grid world environment for instruction following. The observation in BabyAI is 249 a 7 × 7 × 3 grid describing a partial and local egocentric view of the state of the environment. 250 We evaluate the methods on four representative tasks: GoToRedBall , GoToLocal , PickupLoc , and 251 PutNextLocal . Performing well on the test set requires the models to generalize to new environment 252 layouts and goals, resulting in new combinations of tasks not seen in training. For each method, we 253 compute its success rates over 500 episodes on each task. 254

6 Experiments 255

 We first show results of the proposed method and baselines for embodied decision-making tasks using 256 expert data in Section 6.1. We then show our results when using actively gathered data in Section 6.2. 257

6.1 Embodied Decision Making with Pre-trained Language Model (LID)

 258

6.1.1 Results on VirtualHome

 259 We compare the proposed method with a variety of baselines using different policy architectures. 260 LID-Text (Ours) is the proposed method that converts all environments inputs into text descriptions. 261 The pre-trained LM is fine-tuned for decision-making (conditioned on goals, observations, and 262 histories) as described in Section 4.1. 263 Recurrent Network . We compare our method with a recurrent baseline using an LSTM [13] to 264 encode the history information. The hidden representation from the last time step together with the 265 goal, and the current observation are used to predict the next action. 266 MLP and MLP-1 . We perform additional comparisons with baselines that do not use the recurrent 267 network and pre-trained LMs. MLP and MLP-1 take the goal, histories, and the current observation as 268 input and send them to the multilayer perceptron neural network (MLP) to predict actions. MLP-1 has 269 6 three more average-pooling layers than MLP that average the features of tokens in the goal, history 270 actions, and the current observation, respectively, before sending them to the MLP layer. 271 Quantitative results . Each method is trained on 20 K demos from the VirtualHome-Imitation 272 Learning dataset, and then evaluated on the three test subsets: In-Distribution , Novel Scenes , and 273 Novel Tasks . In Figure 3, LID -Text (Ours) , which initializes the policy with a pre-trained LM, 274 has higher success rates than other methods. This difference is most pronounced in the Novel 275 Tasks setting, where test tasks require combinatorial generalization across goals that are never seen 276 during training. Here, LID -Text (Ours) dramatically ( 43 . 6% ) improves upon all baselines. Such 277 combinatorial generalization is necessary to construct general purpose agents, but is often difficult for 278 existing approaches. Our results suggest that pre-trained LMs can serve as a computational backbone 279 for combinatorial generalization. 280

6.1.2 Results on BabyAI 281

 We use the standard training and test data provided by [15]. In BabyAI, performing well on the 282 unseen test tasks with new environment layouts and goals requires approaches having combinatorial 283 reasoning capabilities. In Table 1, we report the success rate of models trained on different number 284 of demos. [15] is the method used in the original paper. LID-Text (Ours) is the proposed method 285 that converts policy inputs into a text sequence. Given enough training data, i.e . 10K demos, both 286 methods achieve high success rates, but LID -Text (Ours) outperforms [15] given fewer training data, 287 indicating the proposed method can generalize well to novel language tasks using fewer training data. 288

7 Analysis: Understanding the Sources of Generalization 318

 The pre-trained LM policy, fine-tuned on either expert data or actively gathered data, exhibits effective 319 combinatorial generalization. Is this simply because LMs are effective models of relations between 320 1 Note that the results of LID-Text in Figure 3 and results of LID-ADG in Table 2 are not directly comparable because the difficulty level of the evaluated tasks are different. See Appendix G for more details. 7 natural language descriptions of states and actions [1], or because they provide a more general 321 framework for combinatorial generalization in decision-making? We hypothesize and investigate 322 three possible factors to understand the sources of such combinatorial generalization. 323

7.1 Input Encoding Scheme

 324 We first hypothesize that converting environment inputs into natural language contributes to the 325 combinatorial generalization as the LMs are trained on language data. We explore the role of natural 326 language by investigating three alternative ways of encoding policy inputs to our model without using 327 natural language strings: two in VirtualHome, and one in BabyAI. BabyAI results are in Appendix A. 328 Index encoding in VirtualHome. Different 329 from LID -Text (Ours) that convert policy inputs 330 into natural language strings, LID -Index (Ours) 331 converts policy inputs into indexes. LID -Index 332 (Ours) retains the discrete, serial format of the 333 goal, history, and observation, but replaces each 334 word with an index, and the embedding layer 335 from the pre-trained LM with a new embedding 336 layer trained from scratch. For example, grab 337 apple is mapped to “5 3” based on the positions 338 of grab and apple in the vocabulary set. 339 Unnatural string encoding in VirtualHome. LID -Unnatural (Ours) replaces the natural language 340 tokens (e.g. converting the goal “ On(fork, table):1 ” as put one fork on the table ) with random 341 ones (e.g. converting On(fork, table) as brought wise character trees fine yet ). This is done by 342 randomly permuting the entire vocabulary, mapping each token to a new token. Such a permutation 343 breaks the semantic information in natural strings. 344 LID -Index (Ours) and LID -Unnatural (Ours) have the same policy network as LID -Text (Ours) . All 345 of them are fine-tuned on the expert data. Each of them is trained on different numbers of demos. The 346 averaged results using 5 different random seeds on the Novel Tasks setting are reported in Table 4. 347 Given few training data, e.g. 100 demos, all the models perform poorly, with success rates lower than 348 10% . LID -Text (Ours) achieves higher success rates than LID -Index (Ours) and LID -Unnatural 349 (Ours) when the training data is increased, e.g . LID -Text (Ours) is around 4% higher than LID -Index 350 (Ours) and LID -Unnatural (Ours) when there are 500 training demos. However, when the training 351 dataset is further enlarged, e.g . 20K demos, success rates of all approaches reach similar performance. 352 Such a result indicates that the effectiveness of pre-trained LMs in compositional generalization is not 353 unique to natural language strings, but can be leveraged from arbitrary encodings, although adapting 354 the model to arbitrary encodings may require more training data. 355

7.2 Sequential Input Representation

 356 Next, we explore whether the generalization is 357 caused by the sequential processing mechanisms in 358 transformer-based LMs. We investigate whether the 359 LM pre-trained policy will still be effective when the 360 input encoding is not sequential. No-Seq uses the 361 non-sequential inputs. It encodes the goal as a single 362 vector by averaging the features of all goal embed- 363 dings. The history and observation features are ob- 364 tained in the same way. All the features are then sent 365 to the pre-trained LM to predict actions. As shown in 366 8 N ov e l T a s k s o T o L o c a l I n - D i s t r i bu t i o n Table 5, removing the sequential structure significantly hurts the performance on Novel Tasks . No-Seq 367 achieves good performance on test tasks that are closer to training tasks, but cannot generalize well to 368 more challenging unseen tasks. Thus, the combinatorial generalization of pre-trained LMs may be 369 attributed in part to the transformer’s ability to process sequential input representations effectively. 370

7.3 Favorable Weight Initialization 371

 Finally, we investigate if the favorable weight initialization from LM pre-training enables effective 372 generalization of the proposed model. No-Pretrain does not initialize the policy using the pre-trained 373 LM, but instead training the policy on the expert data from scratch. In Table 5, we find that removing 374 the pre-trained weights can fit the in-domain data and thus performs well on the In-Distribution 375 setting. However, its success rate is 11 . 2% lower than the proposed model on the Novel Tasks setting, 376 indicating the pre-trained weights are important for effective generalization, but not necessary for 377 effective data fitting. We further test a baseline, No-FT , that keeps the pre-trained weights of the 378 language model but freezes them while training the rest model on our expert data. Freezing the pre- 379 trained weights without fine-tuning significantly hurts the performance on both settings, suggesting 380 that fine-tuning of the transformer weights is essential for effective combinatorial generalization. 381 Together, these results suggest that sequential input representations (vs. fixed-dimensional feature 382 vectors) and favorable weight initialization are both important for generalization, however, the 383 input encoding schemes (e.g. as a natural language string vs. an arbitrary encoding scheme) has 384 little influence. These results point to the potential broader applicability of pre-trained LMs as a 385 computational backbone for compositional embodied decision making, where arbitrary inputs, such 386 as language, images, or grids, may be converted to sequential encodings. 387

9 Conclusion and Broader Impact 393

 In this paper, we introduced LID, a general approach to sequential decision-making that converts 394 goals, histories, and observations into sequences and processes them using a policy initialized with 395 a pre-trained LM. We integrated an active data gathering procedure into the proposed method to 396 enable policy learning without using expert data. Our analysis showed that input representation and 397 favorable weight initialization both contribute to the generalization while the input encoding scheme 398 has little influence. One drawback of the active data gathering is that it relies on hand-designed rules 399 for task relabeling. More generally, a potential disadvantage of the proposed approach is that biases 400 of the pre-trained LMs may influence its behavior, and further study of LID-based models’ bias is 401 required before they may be deployed in sensitive downstream applications. Nevertheless, our results 402 demonstrate that LID enables effective combinatorial generalization across different environments, 403 and highlight the promise of LM pre-training for more general decision-making problems. 404 9

A Convolutional encoding in BabyAI 563

 In the main paper Section 7.1, we explore the role of natural language by investigating two alternative 564 ways of encoding policy inputs in VirtualHome. In this section, we show the third way of encoding 565 policy inputs in BabyAI. 566 We test a new model, LID-Conv (Ours) , that converts environment inputs into convolutional 567 embeddings . We pass the 7 × 7 × 3 grid observation in BabyAI to convolutional layers and obtain 568 a 7 × 7 × d feature map, where d is the feature dimension. We flatten the feature map and get a 569 sequence of features to describe the observation. The rest of the model is the same as LID -Text 570 (Ours) . Table 6 shows the results of policies using the text encoding and convolutional encoding . 571 LID -Text (Ours) and LID -Conv (Ours) have similar results given enough training data, but LID -Text 572 (Ours) is slightly better when there are fewer training data. This conclusion is coincident with the 573 results on VirtualHome. 574 Different input encoding schemes have only a negligible impact on model performance: the effective- 575 ness of pre-training is not limited to utilizing natural strings, but in fact extends to arbitrary sequential 576 encodings. 577

 578 Failure case analysis. In Figure 5, we show some failure cases of the proposed method. We observed two main types of failure cases: grounding error and policy error. For failures caused by the policy error, the agent 582 cannot find the target objects or does not interact with them. C Environments 587

 We use BabyAI [15] and VirtualHome [29] to evaluate the proposed method. While both environ- 588 ments feature complex goals, the nature of these goals, as well as the state and action sequences that 589 accomplish them, differ substantially across environments. 590

C.1 VirtualHome 591

 VirtualHome is a 3D realistic environment featuring partial observability, large action spaces, and 592 long time horizons. It provides a set of realistic 3D homes and objects that can be manipulated to 593 perform household organization tasks. 594 Goal Space. For each task, we define the goal as a set of predicates and multiplicities. For example, 595 Inside(apple, fridge):2 ; Inside(pancake, fridge):1 ; means “put two apples and one 596 pancake inside the fridge”. In each task, the initial environment (including initial object locations), 597 the goal predicates, and their orders and multiplicities are randomly sampled. There are 59 different 598 types of predicates in total. 599 Observation Space. The observation in VirtualHome by default is a graph describing a list of objects 600 and their relations in the current partial observation. Each object has an object name, a state, e.g . 601 open, close, clean , and 3D coordinates. 602 Action Space. Agents can navigate in the environment and interact with objects. To interact with an 603 object, the agent must predict an action name and the index of the interested object, e.g . Open(5) to 604 opening the object with index (5). The agent can only interact with objects that are in the current 605 observation or execute the navigation actions, such as Walk(bathroom) . For some actions, such 606 as open , the agent must be close to the object. There are also strict preconditions for actions, e.g . 607 the agent must grab an object before it can put the object on a target position. As a result of these 608 constraints, the subset of actions available to the agent changes at every timestep. 609 We evaluate the success rates of different methods on VirtualHome. A given episode is scored as 610 successful if the policy completes its entire goal within T steps, where T = 70 is the maximum 611 allowed steps of the environment. 612

C.2 BabyAI

 613 BabyAI is a 2D grid world environment designed to evaluate instruction following. Different from 614 VirtualHome, the observation in BabyAI by default is a grid describing a partial and local egocentric 615 view of the state of the environment. This grid shows 7 × 7 tiles in the direction the agent is facing. 616 Each tile contains at most one object, encoded using 3 integer values: one storing the type of object, 617 one storing its color, and a state for doors indicating whether it is open, closed or locked. The goals 618 in BabyAI are described using language instructions, e.g . “put the blue key next to the purple ball”. 619 BabyAI has 7 actions, e.g . “turn left”, “pick up”, and “drop”. 620 15 Pre-Trained Language Models for Interactive Decision-Making observation into a sequence of image patches as in Vision Transformer (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) We choose to convert the observations goal into and pass them pre language model. We take the text tokens as an example explain the method Goal. Each goal consists of a sequence of predicates and multiplicities, and is translated into a templated English sen- tence ( e.g . “ Inside(apple, fridge):2 ” becomes “put two apples inside the fridge”). Observation. To en- code the agent’s partial observation, we extract a list of currently visible objects, their states ( e.g . “open, clean”), and3Dworldcoordinates. Weuseafully-connectedlayerto encode the 3D information and generate a feature represen- tation of each object in the observation. See Appendix B.1 for more details. History. We store information about all previous actions and convert them into templated English sentences ( e.g . “I have put the plate on the kitchen table and the apple inside the fridge”). Action prediction. VirtualHome features a large action space, and the set of valid actions changes as the agent moves through and interacts with the environment. Each action consists of 1 verb and 1 object. In training, we maxi- mize the probabilities of the verb and object selected by an expert action. To produce the verb probabilities, we pool the outputs of the pre-trained LM and pass this “context feature” through a fully-connected layer as shown in Figure 2. To determine the object probabilities, the model computes the inner product of the context feature with the LM output vec- tors corresponding to each object in the observation. This design automatically ﬁlters out objects that are not in the ob- servation and hence cannot be interacted with. In inference, we select the valid action with the highest joint probability 1 .

D.1 Model

 architecture details in VirtualHome 624 In this section, we provide more details of the policy network we used in VirtualHome. Our policy 625 model consists of three parts, i.e . inputs, the pre-trained LM, and outputs. As shown Figure 6, we 626 encode the inputs to the policy—including goal g , history h t , and the current partial observation o t — 627 as sequences of embeddings. These embeddings are passed to the LM (using its pre-trained embedding 628 layer F θ ) and used to obtain contextualized token representations. These token representations are 629 averaged to generate a context feature f c , which is then passed to fully-connected layer to predict the 630 next action a t +1 . The output action in VirtualHome consists of a verb and an object. For brevity, we 631 omit the time subscript t from now on. 632 In VirtualHome, the partial observation o of the environment state can be represented as a list of 633 objects in the agent’s view. We represent each object by its name, e.g . “oven”, a state description, 634 e.g . “open, clean”, and position both in the world and relative to the agent. In this part, we provide 635 more details of how LID-Text (Ours) encodes the name, state, and position of each object in the 636 observation. Figure 7 shows the model architecture we used to encode the observation. 637 Name encoding. For each object node, we serialize its object name as an English phrase s o . We 638 extract its tokens and features using the tokenizer and the embedding layer of the pre-trained LM, 639 respectively. Since one object name might generate several English tokens using the tokenizer from 640 the pre-trained LM, e.g . the tokens of “kitchencabinet” is [15813 , 6607 , 16212 , 500] , we take the 641 averaged features of all the tokens in the object name and obtain a “name” feature f o, name i for each 642 object node as shown in Figure 7. 643 State encoding. Some objects have a state description, e.g . “oven: open, clean”. There are six types 644 of object states in the environment: “clean”, “closed”, “off”, “on”, “open”, and “none”. For each 645 object node, we use a binary vector to represent its state. Taking the “oven” as an example, if the oven 646 16 f c Observation o t History h t Goal g F 𝜃 F 𝜃 FC FC FC Name (e.g. “kitchen oven”) Statevector Positionvector FC FC FC F 𝜃 FC Token sequence F 𝜃 Avg pool Concatenate For each object in o t FC (𝑥,𝑦,𝑧) (𝑥,𝑦,𝑧) Tokenization ReLU . is open and clean, its state vector would be [1 , 0 , 0 , 0 , 1 , 0] . This state vector is then passed through a 647 fully-connected layer to generate a state feature f o, state i of object o i . 648 Position encoding. To encode the position information of each object o i , we take their world 649 coordinates { o i,x , o i,y , o i,z } and their spatial distance to the agent { a x , a y , a z } to generate a position 650 vector [ o i,x , o i,y , o i,z , o i,x − a x , o i,y − a y , o i,z − a z ] . This position vector is then passed through two 651 fully-connected layers with a ReLU layer in the middle to generate a position feature f o, position i of 652 object o i . 653 The final feature f oi of each object node is obtained by passing the concatenation of its name 654 feature f o, name i , state feature f o, state i , and position feature f o, position i through a fully-connect layer. The 655 observation at a single step can be written as a set of features { f o 1 , · · · , f oN } , where N is the number 656 of objects in the current observation. 657

 Our proposed approach and baselines are trained on Tesla 32GB GPUs. We train every single model 659 on 1 Tesla 32GB GPU. All experiments used the AdamW optimizer with the learning rate of 10 − 5 . 660 We utilize a standard pre-trained language model, GPT-2, in our experiments. GPT-2 is trained on the 661 Webtext dataset [31] using the Huggingface library [42]. 662

F.1 Expert Data Collection

 669 VirtualHome-Imitation Learning Dataset. To train the models, we collect a set of expert trajectories 670 in VirtualHome using regression planning (RP) [20]. We follow the implementation of the regression 671 planner used in [30]. Given a task described by goal predicates, the planner generates an action 672 sequence to accomplish this task. As shown in Figure 8, the agent has a belief about the environment, 673 i.e . an imagined distribution of object locations. As the agent explores the environment, its belief 674 of the world becomes closer to the real world. At every step, the agent updates its belief based on 675 the latest observation (see [30]), finds a new plan using the regression planner, and executes the first 676 action of the plan. If the subtask (described by the goal predicate) has been finished, the agent will 677 select a new unfinished subtask, otherwise, the agent will keep doing this subtask until it finishes. 678 Similarly to previous work [38, 37, 30], we generate training data using a planner that has access 679 to privileged information, such as full observation of the environment and information about the 680 pre-conditions and effects of each action. The planner allows an agent to robustly perform tasks in 681 partially observable environments and generate expert trajectories for training and evaluation. We 682 generate 20 , 000 trajectories for training and 3 , 000 trajectories for validation. Each trajectory has a 683 goal, an action sequence, and the corresponding observations after executing each action. 684 18 Given: a goal relabel function f l ; Initialize: policy π ϕ ; goal set G ; training replay buffer R train = {} ; validation replay buffer R val = {} ; for iteration=1, N do for example=1, M do Sample a goal g from G and an initial state s o ; for t = 0 , T do Sample an action from policy π ϕ ( a t +1 | g, h t , o t ) or sample an action randomly; Execute a t +1 and obtain a new observation o t +1 ; end Store the trajectory ( o 0 , a 0 , · · · , o T , g ) in the replay buffer R train or R val ; end Relabel each failure trajectory d = ( o 0 , a 0 , · · · , o T ) in the replay buffers and get new goal g ′ = f l ( d ) ; Put new goals g ′ in the goal set G ; for k = 1 , K do repeat Sample data from R train and update policy π ϕ ; until training episode ends ; Get validation accuracy using data from R val ; end π ϕ = π val_best end

F.2 Active Data Gathering

 685 The algorithm for active data gathering is shown in Algorithm 2. The hindsight relabeling stage is 686 the key component for active data gathering. In this part, we provide more implementation details of 687 how we relabel “failed” trajectories with new goals in the hindsight relabeling stage. 688 For each “failed” trajectory, we extract its useful sub-trajectories and relabel a task goal g ′ for it. 689 We design a goal relabel function f l that generates a goal based on the sequence of observations 690 and actions. To do this, we first use a hand-designed program to detect what tasks are contained in 691 a “failed” trajectory. This program find useful tasks based on the keywords in the action list. For 692 example in Figure 9, the program knows the trajectory containing a task of “ On(apple, kitchen 693 table) : 1” based on the action “ [ put ] < apple >< kitchentable > ”. 694 The selected sub-trajectories are not always optimal. We thus design a rule to filter out bad trajectories, 695 i.e . for trajectories with the same goal, selecting the “shorter” ones. One example is shown in 696 Figure 10. Suppose that there are two trajectories having the same goal, e.g . “ On(apple, kitchen 697 table) : 1”. The first trajectory has actions that are redundant or not related to the task, such as 698 “ [ walk ] < bathroom > ” and “ [ walk ] < kitchen > ” while the second trajectory is more optimal 699 given the goal. We select the second trajectory and delete the first trajectory from the replay buffer. 700 Note that the “shorter” does not mean fewer actions, but fewer actions that are not related to the task. 701 The hindsight relabeling stage allows sample-efficient learning by reusing the failure cases. The 702 relabeled data are used to train policies in the policy update stage. 703 704

G.2 LID-ADG Test Sets 718

 As we have mentioned in the main paper Section 9, one limitation of active data gathering is that it 719 relies on hand-designed rules for task relabeling. In addition, it is sometimes challenging to define 720 effective rules to extract useful sub-trajectories and get high-quality hindsight labels, especially when 721 trajectories are long and tasks become more complex. Thus we only relabel short sub-trajectories, 722 where the goal consists of a single goal predicate, e.g . “ On(apple, kitchen table) :1”. During 723 testing, we evaluate the success rate of approaches on solving such tasks as well, i.e . the count of the 724 goal predicate equals to 1. The types of goal predicates are still the same as Section G.1, i.e . 37 goal 725 predicates in the In-Distribution setting and the Novel Scenes setting, and 22 goal predicates in the 726 Novel Tasks setting. 727 20

H Visualization of Attention Weights 728

 To better understand how does LM pre-trained policies make decisions, we visualize the attention 729 weights from the self-attention layers of GPT-2 [40] in Figure 11 and Figure 12. We show the 730 attention weights from the input to the output of LID-Text (Ours) . The order of tokens in the input 731 and ouput is observation, goal, and history. 732 Figure 11 illustrates the attention weights of a layer named “Head 3 Layer 2”. We show attention 733 weights on two different tasks. We find that “Head 3 Layer 2” can capture objects in the goal 734 predicates, such as “wineglass” and “cutleryfork” in the left figure, and “pancake” and “chicken” in 735 the right figure (the figures are cropped for visualization). 736 Figure 12 illustrates the attention weights of layers named “Head 1 Layer 2” (left) and “Head 4 Layer 737 11” (right). Given the goal predicates, history, and the current observation, the policy predict the next 738 action as “grab milk”. We find that “Head 1 Layer 2” is able to capture objects in the goal predicates, 739 such as “milk”, “pancake”, and “chicken” while “Head 4 Layer 11” focuses on the interacted object 740 in the predicted action, such as “milk”. 741 The attention weights from different self-attention layers are significantly different—some self- 742 attention layers assign high attention weight to objects in the goal predicates while some layers focus 743 on the interacted object. There are also some layers that do not have interpretable meanings. The 744 attention weights just provide us an intuition of how does the internal language model works, more 745 quantified results are reported in the main paper. 746 21 22 23
